entries.title: Kaiserjäger monument to the war dead in Bolzano, and a figure made for it
text: The Austrian monument to the Kaiserjäger war dead, begun in 1917 on the spot where the Monument to Victory now stands: a drum of rough-hewn stone, never finished. In 1928 the Alpenzeitung recalled that the Austrians had wanted to raise their monument here “in voreiligem Siegesbewußtsein”, in premature certainty of victory.

Its demolition began in spring 1927, by the exhibition's guide (Wikimedia Commons says 1920). One of its figures stands in the crypt as a cast of 2013: Franz Ehrenhöfer's “Soldatentreue”, about 1917, a man bowed over his crossed arms.
facts: Commons: 'Kaiserjäger monument to war dead, built in 1917 and demolished 1920 to make way for the Victory Monument in Bolzano'; photographer unknown, dated ca. 1917–1920 (manifest)
The Victory Monument replaced the unfinished Kaiserjäger monument (Karl Ernstberger, begun 1917), which was demolished [W] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: a round drum of rough-hewn stone blocks with a dark doorway, square blocks standing on its top, a low stone wall in front and a carved figure under an arch at left; bare trees behind.

The Alpenzeitung of 13 July 1928 says the Victory Monument stands 'dort am Grunde der Talferbrücke, wo einst auch die Oesterreicher in voreiligem Siegesbewußtsein ihr Denkmal errichten wollten' (file images/03_vittoria__AZ_1928_07_13_1_SiD.png)

Label in the crypt: 'Franz Ehrenhöfer, The soldier's loyalty, allegorical figure for the Kaiserjäger Monument, ca. 1917. Plaster cast made from concrete original in 2013' / 'La fedeltà del soldato, figura allegorica per il Monumento ai Kaiserjäger, conglomerato cementizio, 1917 ca. (calco 2013)' / 'Soldatentreue, allegorische Figur für das Bozener Kaiserjäger-Denkmal, Steinguss, um 1917 (Abguss 2013)' (own photograph IMG_1749, 14 November 2026; notes 17, §8, [V])

Guide 2024: 'Nell'estate del 1916 l'architetto boemo Karl Ernstberger progettò un monumento in memoria dei molti caduti del II reggimento dei Tiroler Kaiserjäger di stanza a Bolzano'; 'La realizzazione … ebbe inizio solo nel 1917 … e non fu mai completata'; 'La demolizione del Monumento ai Kaiserjäger incominciò nella primavera del 1927, contemporaneamente alle opere di sbancamento per le fondazioni del nuovo Monumento' (row 5.29, [V]). This contradicts the 1920 of Wikimedia Commons given by an earlier version of this row
Innsbrucker Nachrichten, 12 July 1928, p. 2, draws the memorial and captions it 'das bereits fast vollendet war, von den Italienern aber zerstört wurde' (row 17.24, [V])

Seen in the images (crypt, 2026): a grey half-figure of a bare-headed man rising from a round base, bowed forward over crossed arms, his hands gripping a weapon against his left shoulder, an ornamented shield or pommel behind his right; on a dark steel plinth in a corner of the crypt.

entries.title: Sergio Perdomi, first stone of the Victory Monument laid in the presence of Vittorio Emanuele III
text: The laying of the first stone of the Monument to Victory on 12 July 1926, photographed by Sergio Perdomi: a dressed block hanging on chains, a bishop in mitre bowing over it, uniforms and dark suits around. The monument had been decided in February and was designed by Marcello Piacentini. It was inaugurated two years later to the day.
facts: Commons: 'Sergio Perdomi - Groundbreaking of the Monument to Victory in Bolzano with king Victor Emmanuel III', dated 1926 (manifest)
Decided on 10 Feb 1926 and designed by Marcello Piacentini; first stone 12 July 1926; inaugurated 12 July 1928 by Vittorio Emanuele III [W] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: a dressed stone block hangs on chains from a lifting frame; a bishop in mitre and vestments bows over it, men in uniform and in dark suits stand round, festoons hang behind; printed along the bottom: 'BOLZANO 12 LUGLIO 1926'.
The funding subscription raised 3 million lire [V] (notes 05, §3)

images.caption: Sergio Perdomi, 12 July 1926. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

entries.creator: Sergio Perdomi

entries.title: Alpenzeitung, 13 July 1928, page 1
text: The Alpenzeitung's front page on the unveiling of the Monument to Victory. It prints and explains the Latin inscription: “Hic patriae fines, siste signa. Hinc ceteros excoluimus lingua legibus artibus.” Here is the border of the fatherland; from here we civilised the others in language, laws and arts.
The German text is set in Fraktur, the Latin and the headlines in roman type. An earlier draft of the inscription is said to have had “barbaros” where it now says “ceteros”.
facts: Commons: 'The fascist newspaper Alpenzeitung commemorating the inauguration of the Monument to Victory in Bozen-Bolzano, on July 12, 1928 (edition of the following day), explaining also the latin inscriptions'; author unknown (manifest)

Seen in the image: blackletter masthead 'Alpenzeitung', 'Politisches Tagblatt der Provinz Bolzano', 'Freitag, den 13. Juli 1928 – Anno VI', headline 'Die Enthüllung des Siegesdenkmals'; the body text is set in Fraktur, the headlines and the Latin lines in roman type.

Seen in the image: under 'Beim Siegesdenkmal' the page prints 'Hic patriae fines, siste signa / Hinc ceteros excoluimus lingua legibus artibus' and says the monument stands 'am Grunde der Talferbrücke, wo einst auch die Oesterreicher … ihr Denkmal errichten wollten'.
The inscription was dictated by Pietro Fedele; an earlier draft had 'barbaros' [W] (notes 05, §3)
Inaugurated 12 July 1928 by Vittorio Emanuele III [W] (notes 05, §3)
The manifest lists this Teßmann page as held only through the Commons copy (manifest, period newspaper pages)

entries.title: Ponte Druso with its eagles, three photographs of 1932–35
text: Ponte Druso with its eagles, in three photographs. Two are by Mario Gabinio, taken between 1932 and 1935: the three stone arches from the riverbed, with the eagles on their tall stepped pylons above the piers, and a bridge-head with a shallow basin resting on helmets and a carved sword on each face. The third, dated 1933, is by an unknown photographer.

They settle one question and open another. The sources disagree on whether the eagles stood at the corners of the bridge or over its central piers: they stand over the piers. And the date under the basin, which the museum catalogue transcribes as “Mxmxv”, appears to read MCMXV, 1915, the year Italy entered the war. The rights of the third photograph are unclear; check before any reuse.
facts: Catalogue description: '… Particolare Di Una Testata Con Ara Votiva Recante La Data Mxmxv; 1932-1935; stampa alla gelatina bromuro d'argento' (manifest)
The notes take 'Mxmxv' for the catalogue's garbled transcription of a Roman numeral and say to read the photo itself [V, Commons metadata] (notes 05, §1)

Seen in the image: a stone block topped by a shallow round basin resting on helmets; the inscription under the basin appears to read 'MCMXV'; a relief sword on each visible face; a flagpole beside it and, far off at left, an eagle on a pylon.
The end blocks carried imperial shields resting on four helmets, and the sides were decorated with Roman swords [V] (notes 05, §1)
The text of the inscriptions (votive altar date, other inscriptions) was not found (notes 05, §1, Gaps)
Credit 'Mario Gabinio / Fondazione Torino Musei' (manifest, rights caveats)

Catalogue description: 'Bolzano, Ponte Druso - Ponte In Pietra A Tre Arcate Con Gruppi Scultorei Raffiguranti Aquile Poggiate Su Fasci Littori; 1932-1935; stampa alla gelatina bromuro d'argento' (manifest)

Seen in the image: a three-arched stone bridge over a dry riverbed; eagle statues stand on tall stepped pylons above the piers, with a pierced stone parapet between them; houses and a mountain behind.
The four central piers carried sculptures more than 8 m high: fasces holding globes, on which 'troneggiavano gigantesche aquile romane' [V] (notes 05, §1)
Four eagles, sculpted in 1931 by Vittorio Morelli of Ancona [V] (notes 05, §1)
The sources disagree on placement (four corners vs four central piers); the Gabinio photos are the best way to settle it visually (notes 05, §1, Inferences)
Credit 'Mario Gabinio / Fondazione Torino Musei' (manifest, rights caveats)
Commons: 'Drususbrücke 1933', dated 1933-01-01, CC BY 4.0, uploader Bartleby08 (manifest)
Tagged CC BY 4.0 'own work' by Bartleby08 although it shows a 1933 view; real author and rights unclear, verify before reuse (manifest, rights caveats; notes 05, §1)

Seen in the image: the three-arched stone bridge seen from the gravel riverbed; eagle statues on tall stepped pylons rise above the piers; a pierced stone parapet; a small round stamp in the lower left corner.
The bridge opened to traffic on 28 October 1931, the ninth anniversary of the March on Rome [V] (notes 05, §1)
Four eagles by Vittorio Morelli (1931) stood on fasces holding globes over the four central piers [V] (notes 05, §1)

entries.title: Theodor Eicke and Italian fascist authorities at the Victory Monument
text: 28 October 1932, the tenth anniversary of the March on Rome, at the Monument to Victory. A man in uniform with a swastika armband shakes hands with an Italian officer. He is identified as Theodor Eicke, an SS leader then hiding in Italy from the German police, who took part in the ceremony with thirty SS men.
The identification and the date are those of Wikimedia Commons and Wikipedia.
facts: Commons: 'Theodor Eicke and Italian fascist authorities at the inauguration of the fascist monument of victory in Bolzano, Italy. While hiding from German police in Italy, Eicke took part in a celebration of the 10th anniversary of the fascist "March on Rome"'; dated 1932, scaled copy (manifest)
On 28 Oct 1932 the SS leader Theodor Eicke and 30 SS men took part in the March-on-Rome tenth-anniversary ceremony at the monument [W] (notes 05, §3)

Not the first such scene: a pamphlet printed in Munich in July 1932 reports that three German National Socialists laid a wreath at the Monument on 9 December 1931, 'in Anwesenheit fascistischer Milizleute', and that the party's Bolzano group was founded on 21 January 1932 at the Gasthaus Pfau in the Bindergasse with Fascist militia officers as guests. One polemical source, its own sources not yet opened (Steinberger, p. 44; row 17.06; notes 17, §4.9, [V] for the wording)

Seen in the image: a man in uniform with a swastika armband and a peaked cap shakes hands with an Italian officer in a tall cap; officers in fur caps and dress uniforms with swords and men in civilian coats stand round; a pillar of the monument with a niche rises behind.
Declared PD as an anonymous work; check the Italian and EU rules for anonymous photographs before publication (manifest, rights caveats)

images.caption: Unknown photographer, 1932. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

confidence.note: The Commons description calls the event both the monument's inauguration (1928) and the 10th anniversary of the March on Rome (1932); the date 28 October 1932 comes from it.wikipedia [W].

entries.title: Advertisement “Während der Bozner Messe”, 10 September 1948
text: A newspaper advertisement for the first post-war Bolzano fair, September 1948: flags, a car, strolling visitors and a colonnaded building under the banner “Während der Bozner Messe”. The fair was held at the Palazzo di Giustizia on Piazza Tribunale.
The manifest dates the advertisement 1949. The notes and its own title say 1948.
facts: Commons: 'Bozner Messe Gerichtsplatz 1948', Bartleby08, CC BY 4.0, dated 1949-09-10 (manifest)
The notes list it as 'the 1948 fair on Piazza Tribunale (Dolomiten)' (notes 05, §3, images)
The Palazzo di Giustizia hosted the first postwar Bolzano Fair on 12 Sept 1948 [W] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: a drawn banner 'Während der Bozner Messe –' over flags on poles, a car, strolling visitors and a colonnaded building, mountains behind; a lower ribbon reads 'Gute Unterkünfte: Unterhaltung · gepflegte Küche · Ausflugsziele'.

images.caption: Newspaper advertisement, 10 September 1948; uploaded by Bartleby08 as CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

confidence.note: Commons credits Bartleby08 with CC BY 4.0 for a 1948 advertisement; the manifest dates it 1949-09-10 against 1948 in its description and file name; the notes name Dolomiten, the file code is DS.

entries.title: Postcard of Ponte Druso with the eagles, 1960s
text: A colour postcard of the 1960s looking along the roadway of Ponte Druso. On both sides the eagles stand on balls atop tall ribbed pylons of reddish stone; small cars pass, and a man walks on the pavement.
The regime had been gone for about twenty years. The eagles came down in the following decade.
facts: Commons: 'postcard - bolzano - ponte druso - anni '60', public domain via Flickr; author given as 'paolo from tv, preganziol', date 2024-07-12 (manifest)
A 1960s postcard with the eagles still in place [V] (notes 05, §1)

Seen in the image: a colour view along the bridge roadway; on both sides eagle statues stand on balls atop tall ribbed pylons of reddish stone; small cars on the cobbled road, a man walking on the pavement, a long yellow building at the far end and jagged mountains behind.
The eagles came down in the 1970s renovation; the year is unresolved: 1972, early 1970s, around 1970 or mid-1970s (notes 05, §1)
Declared public domain on Commons; check the Italian and EU rules before publication (manifest, rights caveats)

images.caption: Postcard, 1960s; scan by paolo from tv, preganziol. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

entries.title: Città di Bolzano, explanatory plaques for the Victory Monument in four languages
text: Four steel plaques placed by the city across the road from the Monument to Victory, in Italian, German, Ladin and English. The Italian one begins: “Questo monumento fu eretto durante il regime fascista per celebrare la vittoria dell'Italia nella Prima Guerra Mondiale.” It was the first step of adding words to the monument instead of taking stone away.
The plaques themselves are dated 2004. The notes, following Wikipedia, say 2005.
facts: Commons: 'Erklärtafeln zum Bozner Siegesdenkmal von 2004', photographed 2023-11-02 by Zintosch7, CC0 (manifest)
it.wikipedia lists 'the 2005 explanatory plaques in four languages placed about 50 m away' in the monument's later history [W] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: four steel plaques on dark posts in a flowerbed, each headed 'Città di Bolzano – Stadt Bozen' and dated 2004, in Italian, German, Ladin and English; across the road stands the monument, a red band round one of its columns.

Seen in the image: the Italian plaque reads 'Questo monumento fu eretto durante il regime fascista per celebrare la vittoria dell'Italia nella Prima Guerra Mondiale. Essa comportò anche la divisione del Tirolo …' and 'La Città di Bolzano, libera e democratica, condanna le divisioni e le discriminazioni del passato e ogni forma di nazionalismo …'.
Before the 2011 Bondi–SVP agreement came a 1978 bomb, the 2002 referendum and the 2005 plaques (notes 05, §4, Takeaway)

entries.title: Bolzano. Percorso tra architettura e fascismo
text: The Comune's own guide to its fascist architecture, with texts by Martha Verdorfer: one route on foot from the station by Ponte Druso to Piazza Vittoria, one by bicycle through the Semirurali and the Rione Littorio. It is the most complete itinerary of its kind found, and the main source for the bridge: “Alla metà degli anni Settanta … furono eliminate tutte le parti con riferimenti ideologici.”
On the Cinema Corso: “La demolizione dell'edificio nel 1988 fu deplorata da molti cittadini.”
facts: The Comune's self-guided route, texts by Martha Verdorfer: route 1 on foot or by bike (station → Ponte Druso → Piazza Vittoria) and cycling route 2 (Semirurali, Rione Littorio); 'the most complete "dark heritage" itinerary found' [V] (notes 05, §5)
Imprint: 'Arti Grafiche Saturnia s.a.s. - TN, novembre 2007', 'Testi: Martha Verdorfer', '© Comune di Bolzano, Assessorato alla Cultura, Ufficio Servizi museali e storico-artistici' (file, p. 1)

Main source on Ponte Druso: work began in March 1930 for the A.A.S.S.; fasces holding globes with 'gigantesche aquile romane'; 'Alla metà degli anni Settanta … furono eliminate tutte le parti con riferimenti ideologici' [V] (notes 05, §1)
On the Cinema Corso (Armando Ronca, 1938): 'Nel 1988 l'edificio fu demolito'; 'La demolizione dell'edificio nel 1988 fu deplorata da molti cittadini' [V] (notes 05, §2)
Calls the stadium's Drusus name 'uno dei molti esempi di strumentalizzazione fascista della storia romana' [V] (notes 05, §1)

entries.title: Die Architektur für ein italienisches Südtirol 1922–1943
text: Harald Dunajtschik and Gerald Steinacher on architecture as the instrument of an Italian South Tyrol: “Das mehrheitlich deutschsprachige Südtirol sollte mehrheitlich italienisch werden.”

The article is the source for the Drusus myth, for Tolomei's wish to replace the statue of Walther with one of Drusus, and for the relief on the Casa del Fascio, dated to the twentieth year of the regime, with the Duce on horseback and “credere, obbedire, combattere”. German speakers called the Semirurali “Schanghai”.
facts: H. Dunajtschik & G. Steinacher, 'Die Architektur für ein italienisches Südtirol 1922–1943', Geschichte und Region/Storia e regione 17 (2008) 1, pp. 101–137 (notes 05, §1)

Fascist propaganda claimed Bozen was founded by Drusus; Tolomei demanded a Drusus monument in place of the Walther statue; Mussolini refused, and in 1926 Piazza Walther was only renamed 'Piazza Vittorio Emanuele III' [V] (notes 05, §1)
The Piffrader relief is dated 'EF XX' (1942) and shows the Duce on horseback with the PNF, GIL, GUF, OND and MVSN acronyms and 'credere, obbedire, combattere' [V] (notes 05, §3)
Zona Industriale opened 20 Dec 1936 (Lancia, Falck, Montecatini); Rione Littorio from 1935; Rione Dux / 'Semirurali' from 1937, stigmatised by German speakers as 'Schanghai' [V] (notes 05, §3)
'Eine herausragende Rolle spielte dabei die Architektur. Das mehrheitlich deutschsprachige Südtirol sollte mehrheitlich italienisch werden.' (file, p. 1)

entries.title: Street signs of the square: “Piazza della Vittoria (già Piazza della Pace) / Siegesplatz (ehem. Friedensplatz)” and the “Piazza della Pace” sign it replaced
entries.date: 22 May 2009; the earlier sign photographed 14 November 2026
text: A street sign on Piazza Vittoria: “Piazza della Vittoria (già Piazza della Pace) / Siegesplatz (ehem. Friedensplatz)”. The city renamed the square Peace Square at the end of 2001. A referendum in October 2002, which most German speakers boycotted, restored the old name with 61.94% of the vote.
The sign keeps both names; the failed renaming is recorded in brackets. The sign of the months in between, “Piazza della Pace / Friedensplatz”, now hangs as an exhibit in the crypt of the monument.
facts: Commons: 'Strassenschild der Gemeinde Bozen am Siegesplatz (ehemaliger Friedensplatz)', HaTe, 2009-05-22, scaled copy (manifest)

In December 2001 the city government renamed Piazza della Vittoria 'Piazza della Pace'; after a consultative referendum in October 2002, which most German speakers boycotted, 'Sì' won with 61.94% and the old name was restored; a sign was added: 'Già della Pace' [W] (notes 05, §3)
Carlà & Mitterhofer date the council decision to 2002 [V] (notes 05, §3)
Seen in the image: a pale plaque on a pebble-render wall reading 'PIAZZA della VITTORIA (già Piazza della Pace) / SIEGESPLATZ (ehem. Friedensplatz)'.

The sign of 2001–02 is shown in BZ '18–'45 beside a panel headed 'La comunità rilegge il monumento' / 'Die Gemeinschaft versteht das Denkmal neu' (own photograph IMG_1782, 14 November 2026; notes 17, §8, [V])

Seen in the image (crypt, 2026): a white street sign with a blue rim and a red dot, lettered in black 'Piazza della Pace / Friedensplatz', fixed to the wall of the exhibition; a dark text panel below at left.

entries.title: Commissione per il percorso espositivo all'interno del Monumento alla Vittoria di Bolzano
text: The paper of the historical commission appointed in March 2011 by the State, the Province and the Comune to plan an exhibition inside the Monument to Victory, signed in Bolzano on 2 May 2011. Its principle: not “ipotesi iconoclaste” but “un intervento di spiegazione e contestualizzazione storica del manufatto”. Explain, and do not demolish.

entries.title: Vollmond11, the Lido of Bolzano from above
text: The municipal open-air pool of Bolzano from above, 2013. It was designed by Ettore Sottsass senior and Willy Weyhenmeyer and opened in 1932 for 2,000 bathers. One of the regime's buildings still in everyday use.

entries.title: Gruppe Gut with Jeffrey T. Schnapp, LED ring around a column of the Monument to Victory
text: A ring of red running text clamped round one fasces column of the Monument to Victory, by the designers Gruppe Gut with Jeffrey Schnapp, for the exhibition that opened inside the monument on 21 July 2014. In their own words: “Una scritta led ad anello attorno a una colonna littoria … incide sulla monumentalità e la vanifica.” Schnapp: “by unbalancing, the ring rebalances”. It was also the cheapest of the options.

The second picture shows it at night. Across the top runs the Latin of 1928 in stone capitals. Low on one column the ring runs “ONE MONUMENT, ONE CITY, TWO DICTATORSHIPS” in red light, English first so that neither local language leads. Two inscriptions on one building, eighty-six years apart, in two kinds of lettering.
facts: Commons: 'The Led sign indicating the permanent historical exhibition within the Monument to Victory in Bolzano-Bozen', Bartleby08, 2014-07-29 (manifest)
The LED ring on one fasces column is a 'nose ring for Fascist rhetoric' (Schnapp: 'by unbalancing, the ring rebalances'), chosen partly because it was cheaper than the alternatives [V] (notes 05, §4)
Gruppe Gut: 'Una scritta led ad anello attorno a una colonna littoria … incide sulla monumentalità e la vanifica' [V] (notes 05, §4)

Seen in the image: a dark ring carrying red light lettering (…Z'18- visible, the first letter cut by its curve) fixed round a fluted white column; at left a pale sculpted head on a pedestal, at right a dark bronze nude figure in a niche.
The exhibition BZ '18–'45 opened on 21 July 2014 [V] (notes 05, §4)
Commons: 'The Monument to Victory in Bozen-Bolzano at night', Bartleby08, 2018-01-23 (manifest)

Seen in the image: the floodlit monument at night, across the top 'HIC PATRIAE FINES SISTE SIGNA / HINC CETEROS EXCOLVIMVS LINGVA LEGIBVS ARTIBVS'; low on one column the ring runs red text: 'ONE MONUMENT, ONE CITY, T…', 'UN MONUMENT…', '…STADT, ZWEI DIKTATUREN'; a blurred flare of light covers the upper left.
The Latin inscription was dictated by Pietro Fedele; an earlier draft had 'barbaros' [W] (notes 05, §3)
English is placed first on signs to avoid giving primacy to either local language; Ladin was added later [V] (notes 05, §4)

entries.title: Progetto di allestimento per un percorso espositivo nel Monumento alla Vittoria di Bolzano
text: The design document for the exhibition in the Monument to Victory, by the Bolzano studio Gruppe Gut with Jeffrey Schnapp of Harvard as consultant, dated the day the exhibition opened. It builds on the historians' project in three parts: a path inside, a path outside, and “Cos'è un monumento?” The LED ring is specified here.

entries.title: PtrQs, Ponte Druso today, looking towards the Eurac buildings
text: Ponte Druso in 2014. The balustrade is broken by square stone posts with shallow bowls on top, and by lamp posts. Nothing stands on the posts.

The parapet is a copy from the 1990s, put up after the renovation of the 1970s had removed the original along with the eagles. At the far end is the former Fascist youth building, in Pompeian red, now a research centre.
facts: Commons: 'Bolzano, buildings of Eurac Research in Italian Rationalist architecture', 2014-08-14, scaled copy (manifest)

Seen in the image: the bridge roadway and a pavement of reddish slabs; the pale balustrade is broken by square stone posts topped with shallow bowls, and by modern lamp posts; no statues on the posts; a red building with a tower stands at the far end.
The eagles came down during the 1970s renovation; in the 1990s the bridge was widened and given a new parapet in imitation of the old one (notes 05, §1, Takeaway)

The 1970s 'stylistic washing' removed the stone parapet and Morelli's statues; after public criticism a 1990s widening added a parapet and ornaments resembling the originals [V, abstract] (notes 05, §1)
The ex-GIL by Mansutti and Miozzo, in 'rosso pompeiano', was refurbished for Eurac from the end of 1998 [V] (notes 05, §2)

entries.title: Transforming a Controversial Heritage: The Case of the Fascist Victory Monument in South Tyrol
text: Andrea Carlà and Johanna Mitterhofer of Eurac Research on how the Monument to Victory was transformed. A clause of non-interference shielded the historians' commission from the three governments that paid. English comes first on the signs, and quotations from Arendt, Brecht and Paine are projected over the frescoes of the crypt.
It is the source for the “nose ring” reading of the LED ring and for Schnapp's “by unbalancing, the ring rebalances”.
facts: A. Carlà & J. Mitterhofer, AUC Studia Territorialia 17/2 (2017), pp. 11–34, DOI 10.14712/23363231.2018.1; published 2017, online 2018 (notes 05, §4; manifest)
The 2014 opening followed a 2012 co-funding agreement of the three governments; a non-interference clause shielded the commission [V] (notes 05, §4)
English placed first on signs, Ladin added later; three 'paths'; quotes from Arendt, Brecht and Paine projected over Cadorin's crypt frescoes [V] (notes 05, §4)
The LED ring is a 'nose ring for Fascist rhetoric' (Schnapp: 'by unbalancing, the ring rebalances'), chosen partly because it was cheaper [V] (notes 05, §4)
Dates the council's renaming of Piazza della Vittoria to 2002, where it.wikipedia has December 2001 (notes 05, §3)

entries.title: Wolfgang Moroder, the church of Cristo Re
text: The church of Cristo Re, by Guido Pelizzari and Luigi Colombo, 1938–40: a round bell tower of rough stone, added after the war, and a sculpted Trinity over the door. With the Casa Littoria and the courthouse it forms what has been called the fascist “triade”.
Christ's gesture of blessing has been read as a disguised Roman salute. That reading comes from Wikipedia.
facts: Commons: 'Christ the King Church in Bolzano South Tyrol.', 2017-03-27 (manifest)

Guido Pelizzari and Luigi Colombo, 1938–40; the bell tower was added after the war; the façade Trinity is by Ignaz Gabloner (1939–40), and Christ's blessing gesture has been read as a disguised Roman salute [W] (notes 05, §3)
With the Casa Littoria and the courthouse it forms the fascist 'triade' [W]; the only protected building of the ensemble [V] (notes 05, §2, §3)

Seen in the image: a tall round bell tower of rough stone with a green copper spire; the church front, half hidden by a tree, with a round window and a sculpted group above the door; parked cars in front.

entries.title: Start frei für die Restaurierung der Fassade des historischen Sitzes der Sparkasse
text: A press release of the Südtiroler Sparkasse on restoring the facade of its historic seat. The building of 1904–07 was stripped and re-clad in the 1930s in clinker brick and travertine, with reliefs of fascist symbols by Piffrader. The release says nothing about explaining them. This research counts the facade among what has not been defused.
facts: 'Pressemitteilung vom 20. September 2017' of the Südtiroler Sparkasse on restoring the facade of its historic seat (manifest; file, p. 1)

The Cassa di Risparmio headquarters (Wilhelm Kürschner, 1904–07) was stripped and re-clad in the 1930s with Piffrader reliefs of fascist symbols; listed since 1988; restored 2017–18 [V] (notes 05, §3)
The press release says nothing about contextualisation; the facade is counted among what was not defused [V] (notes 05, §4)

entries.title: Bartleby08, NOI Techpark in the former Alumix aluminium plant
text: The former Alumix aluminium works in the industrial zone in 2017: a brick hall with tall windows beside a new black block, and a painted water tower. The plant of the 1930s closed in the early 1990s. Its remaining buildings were listed in 2004 and reopened in 2017 as a technology park.
facts: Commons: 'Techpark Bozen Bolzano-South Tyrol, former Alumix buildings', 2017-10-21 (manifest)

The Montecatini/Alumix aluminium plant (dated variously 1936, 1937 or 1938) was decommissioned in the early 1990s; its remaining buildings were listed in 2004 and reused for NOI Techpark, opened 2017 [S] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: a brick industrial building with tall windows beside a black block banded in dark stone and glass; a water tower painted with black-and-white patterns; wooden pavilions with tables on a lawn, people; a crane at right, a mountain cliff behind.
The losses of the fascist city came from speculation, housing renewal, deindustrialisation (Alumix) and, in 2026, structural failure (notes 05, §3, Inferences)

entries.title: Arnold Holzknecht and Michele Bernardi, Hannah Arendt's sentence across the relief of the Casa del Fascio
text: Since November 2017 a line of lit white letters runs the whole length of Hans Piffrader's relief on the former Casa del Fascio: “KEIN MENSCH HAT DAS RECHT ZU GEHORCHEN – NESSUNO HA IL DIRITTO DI OBBEDIRE”, and the same in Ladin. Nobody has the right to obey: Hannah Arendt in a radio interview of 1964, set against the relief's “credere, obbedire, combattere”. The work is by Arnold Holzknecht and Michele Bernardi, chosen from 486 entries to a competition of ideas in 2011.

The pictures show it at night; in detail, where the new sans-serif letters hang on a steel bar across the carved PNF and OND; the facade eight months earlier, with nothing written across its 57 panels and 36 metres; and the bench on the square that explains it in four languages. The artists set the “minimalism” of their intervention against the “grandiloquence” of the fascist style. One alphabet has been hung across another.
facts: Commons: 'Facade of the former headquarter of the Fascist party in Bozen-Bolzano now displaying a quote by Hannah Arendt (2018)', 2018-11-06, scaled copy (manifest)

Seen in the image: at night a line of lit white capitals runs the full length of the relief, 'DEGUNI NE À L DËRT DE ULGHÉ – KEIN MENSCH HAT DAS RECHT ZU GEHORCHEN – NESSUNO HA IL DIRITTO DI OBBEDIRE'; below the relief, 'PALAZZO DEGLI UFFICI FINANZIARI / GEBÄUDE DER FINANZÄMTER'.
The notes give the Ladin line as 'Degnu n'a l dërt de ulghè' [V] (notes 05, §4)
An illuminated Hannah Arendt quotation in three languages over the Piffrader relief (November 2017); Bolzano's approach is to add rather than remove (notes 05, §4, Takeaway)
Before it: a legal complaint (esposto) to the prosecutor (Oct 2016), and opposition from Italia Nostra and from Vittorio Sgarbi (Sept 2017) [W] (notes 05, §4)
Commons: 'Arendt vs Mussolini Bozen-Bolzano 2017', Bartleby08, dated 2019-05-24 (manifest)

Seen in the image: white three-dimensional sans-serif capitals 'ECHT ZU GE' fixed on a metal bar held by cables, in front of the travertine relief; behind them the carved letters 'PNF' and 'OND' and carved figures.

Text: 'Kein Mensch hat das Recht zu gehorchen – Nessuno ha il diritto di obbedire – Degnu n'a l dërt de ulghè', from Arendt's radio interview with Joachim C. Fest of 9 Nov 1964, set against the relief's 'credere, obbedire, combattere' [V] (notes 05, §4)
Chosen from 486 entries to the 2011 ideas competition, the Holzknecht–Bernardi project was built with modifications; the installation dates from November 2017, with an info point [V] (notes 05, §4)
The relief, dated EF XX (1942), shows the Duce on horseback with the PNF, GIL, GUF, OND and MVSN acronyms [V] (notes 05, §3)
Commons: 'Palazzo degli Uffici Finanziari Palace on Piazza del Tribunale, Bozen, South Tyrol. (en:Casa del Fascio (Bolzano))', 2017-03-27, scaled copy (manifest)
The notes list it as the Casa Littoria 'before 2017' (notes 05, §3, images)

Seen in the image: the travertine front with the long relief in two rows under a deep cornice, nothing written across it; below, 'PALAZZO DEGLI UFFICI FINANZIARI / GEBÄUDE DER FINANZÄMTER'; red site fencing in front of the entrance; a green-spired bell tower behind at left.

Built 1939–42 by Guido Pelizzari, Francesco Rossi and Luis Plattner; State finance offices since the war; Piffrader's travertine relief has 57 panels, 36 m long, 198 m², about 95 t; 3 panels were installed only in 1957 [V/W] (notes 05, §3)
Moroder asks to be credited as author; the image 'is not in the public domain' (manifest, creator field)
Commons: 'Description of the Bas-Relief in Bozen-Bolzano', Bartleby08, 2017-11-06, scaled copy (manifest)

Seen in the image: a long white bench-like block on the cobbles; a red label 'BZ 'Light on dictatorships / Lum su la ditatures / Licht auf Diktaturen / Luce sulle dittature'; the heading 'The monumental bas-relief in Bozen-Bolzano: from Hans Piffrader to Hannah Arendt' in English, Italian, German and Ladin; 'The bas-relief: the history of fascism in images'; a QR code; large letters 'DEGUNI NE À L DËRT' along the front.
The installation dates from November 2017, with an info point [V] (notes 05, §4)
At the Victory Monument, English is placed first on signs to give primacy to neither local language [V] (notes 05, §4)

What it is: the 2017 intervention on the bas-relief of the former Casa del Fascio, made on the initiative of the South Tyrolean Provincial Administration, on a joint historical commission's proposal, to historicize and recontextualize the relief (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_del_Fascio_(Bolzano)).

Chat: Arnold Holzknecht and Michele Bernardi placed an illuminated Hannah Arendt quote, 'No one has the right to obey', in Italian, German and Ladin. Confirmed by Wikipedia: an illuminated inscription on their project, 'in three languages (Italian, German, Ladin)'; the Guardian gives the sentence as 'Nobody has the right to obey' and calls the inscription LED-illuminated (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa_del_Fascio_(Bolzano); https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2017/dec/06/bolzano-italian-town-defuse-controversial-monuments).

Chat: placed over the 'Credere, obbedire, combattere' relief. Confirmed by both pages: the Guardian says it is superimposed upon the bas-relief of Mussolini on horseback bearing that slogan (https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2017/dec/06/bolzano-italian-town-defuse-controversial-monuments).

Chat: their minimal lettering was deliberately set against the grandiloquence of the fascist style. Confirmed by the Guardian, citing the artists' explanatory text: the 'minimalism' of the intervention is meant to contrast the 'grandiloquence' of the fascist-era style. The Guardian says 'intervention' where the chat says 'lettering' (https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2017/dec/06/bolzano-italian-town-defuse-controversial-monuments).

The Guardian (Carlo Invernizzi-Accetti, 6 December 2017): the quotation is meant as a 'direct answer' to the slogan's 'invitation to blind obedience'; the intervention almost completely failed to generate controversy (https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2017/dec/06/bolzano-italian-town-defuse-controversial-monuments).

The picture is the photograph already held in the Bolzano landmarks folder, Bartleby08, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons (05_landmarks_heritage manifest); used here through a relative path, not downloaded again (manifest).
Seen in the image: large white block letters '...ECHT ZU GE...' fixed to a steel bar that runs across the carved relief; behind them the carved letters 'PNF' and a figure on horseback (manifest).

entries.title: Bartleby08, Corso Libertà at night
text: Corso Libertà at night, 2019: arcaded stone buildings and a bilingual street sign. The avenue was laid out from 1935 under Piacentini's plan, with arcades “molto più grandi” than the medieval ones of the old town.

It has been Corso Littorio, Corso dell'Impero, Corso IX Maggio and, in 1943–45, 9.-Mai-Straße. It became Corso della Libertà only after 1945. The side street on the sign still carries the name of Padre Reginaldo Giuliani, one of the nationalist and war names that were kept.
facts: Commons: 'View of Bozen-Bolzano's Liberty Boulevard 2019', 2019-11-25, scaled copy (manifest)
Laid out from 1935/36 under Piacentini's plan; opened to traffic in 1938 with arcades 'molto più grandi' than the medieval ones [W/V] (notes 05, §3)
Named Corso Littorio, Corso dell'Impero, 'Corso IX Maggio' (after the 9 May 1936 proclamation of the Empire), '9.-Mai-Straße' in 1943–45; Corso della Libertà only after 1945 [W/V] (notes 05, §3)
Seen in the image: a night view along a street of arcaded stone buildings; on an arcade pier a bilingual sign 'via P. R. Giuliani / P.-R.-Giuliani-Str.'; lit decorations hang over the street.
Padre Reginaldo Giuliani is among the nationalist and war names kept after 1945 [W] (notes 05, §3)

entries.title: Palazzo di Giustizia, the west front and the Justitia relief
text: The Palazzo di Giustizia in two photographs. The west front, in November 2025, carries its inscription across the top: “PRO ITALICO IMPERIO VIRTVTE IVSTITIA HIERARCHIA VNGVIBVS ET ROSTRIS”. For the Italian empire, by valour, justice and hierarchy, with claws and beaks. The building was begun in 1939, halted in 1942 and inaugurated in 1956 by the President of the Republic. The inscription “has never been contextualized”.

The relief over the entrance, by Alcide Ticò, shows a man with a tablet marked LEX, a seated Justice with scales and a youth with a sword. This Justice wears no blindfold. Her open eyes look across the square at Mussolini on horseback on the facade opposite. Eight months after the first photograph the centre of the building collapsed (row 5.32).
facts: Commons: 'Justitia bas-relief on Bozen-Bolzano's courthouse 1939', 2020-02-03 (manifest)
The Justitia pediment by Alcide Ticò has no blindfold and looks across at the Mussolini relief [W] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: three carved figures in a frame, a bearded man holding a tablet 'LEX', a seated woman with open, uncovered eyes holding scales, and a young man with a sword; below, 'IVSTITIA' in large capitals.
An it.wikipedia caption credits the Ponte Druso symbolism to Ticò rather than Morelli, which may be a mix-up with this relief [W] (notes 05, §1)
Commons: 'Facciata rivolta verso ovest del palazzo di giustizia di Bolzano', 2025-11-03 (manifest)

By Paolo Rossi de Paoli and Michele Busiri Vici; begun 1939, halted 1942, resumed 1951, inaugurated 15 Sept 1956 by President Gronchi; passed from the State to the Province in December 2017 [W] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: across the top 'PRO ITALICO IMPERIO VIRTVTE IVSTITIA HIERARCHIA VNGVIBVS ET ROSTRIS'; a colonnade of eight square pillars, a relief over the central door, a tall pillar with round medallions on each side of a broad flight of steps; people sitting on the steps.
The courthouse inscription 'has never been contextualized' [V] (notes 05, §4)
Photographed before the partial collapse of 16 July 2026 (manifest; notes 05, §3)

entries.title: Boboseiptu, the Stadio Druso entrance after the 2020–22 renovation
text: The entrance of the Stadio Druso after the renovation of 2020–22: the old gate block with its plaque, “Campo sportivo Druso / Sportplatz”, between new grandstand wings. Stadium and bridge were inaugurated together in 1931, and both kept the name of Drusus after 1945.
The Comune's own guide calls the name “uno dei molti esempi di strumentalizzazione fascista della storia romana”.

A. Nolli, municipal technical office; 1,000-seat stand, 3,000 capacity [V] (notes 05, §3)

entries.title: Bartleby08, fracture in the architrave of the Victory Monument
text: A corner of the Monument to Victory in August 2025. Part of the stone facing has come away and shows the brickwork underneath, beside a carved helmeted head. A crack in the architrave has been open since 2019.

entries.title: Italien im Ersten Weltkrieg, im Faschismus und unter deutscher Besatzung (1915–1945): Geschichte, Erinnerung und Vermittlung. Bericht zur Exkursion 24.05.–30.05.2026
text: The report of a German university excursion that visited the exhibition in the Monument to Victory on 24 May 2026. The students criticise fascist “civilising” language quoted without comment, and note that the colonial column of 1938 and the Virgil inscription on Piazza Vittoria are “nicht erklärt”.
A city councillor told them of a “spürbare Rechtsruck seit 2025”. It is the most recent outside view of how the defusing is holding up.
facts: Student excursion report of the FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg chair of history didactics; excursion 24–30 May 2026 to Bozen, Passo Pordoi, Rovereto, Fossoli, Cumiana and Turin; lecturers Nadja Bennewitz and Leonard Stöcklein (manifest; file, p. 1)
The group visited BZ '18–'45 on 24 May 2026 and criticised some uncritically quoted fascist 'civilising' language and the lack of context for the videos [V] (notes 05, §4)
The colonial 'Ehrensäule' (1938) and the Virgil inscription on the INA building on Piazza Vittoria are 'nicht erklärt', with colonial crimes not named [V] (notes 05, §4)
Describes Hannes Obermair as 'der das Museum konzipierte' [V] (notes 05, §4)
An SVP city councillor told the students of a 'spürbare Rechtsruck seit 2025' [V] (notes 05, §5)
Mentions a visit to the 'Militärfriedhof St. Jakob', which needs follow-up (notes 05, §3, Gaps)

entries.title: Bartleby08, the Palazzo di Giustizia after the collapse of July 2026
text: The Palazzo di Giustizia on 17 July 2026, the day after its central wing collapsed during work on the load-bearing columns. The colonnade still stands with the inscription intact above it: “…VIRTVTE IVSTITIA HIERARCHIA VNGVIBVS ET ROSTRIS”. Behind the pillars is rubble, and through the gap the hills. One cleaner was slightly injured.
Günther Pallaver said the fascist monuments were never really de-fascistised after 1945, and “das rächt sich jetzt”.
facts: Commons: 'Gerichtsgebäude Bozen Juli 2026 nach Einsturz', 2026-07-17, scaled copy (manifest)
On 16 July 2026 the central four-storey courtroom wing behind the colonnade collapsed shortly after 6 a.m. during work on the load-bearing columns; one cleaner was slightly injured [V] (notes 05, §3)
Günther Pallaver: the fascist monuments were never really de-fascistised after 1945, and 'das rächt sich jetzt' [V] (notes 05, §3)

Seen in the image: the colonnade still stands with '…VIRTVTE IVSTITIA HIERARCHIA VNGVIBVS ET ROSTRIS' intact above it; behind the pillars the building has fallen into a heap of rubble, timber and twisted roofing, with terraced green hills visible through the gap; debris on the steps, a fence and red-and-white tape in front.
Five people were placed under investigation for negligent disaster (Aug 2026) [S]; proposals followed for a 'kritische Rekonstruktion' and an institute for fascism research [W] (notes 05, §3)

entries.title: Ponte Druso “prima e dopo la cura”, two photographs in Tandem, gennaio 1985
text: Two photographs printed one above the other in Tandem, January 1985, under the caption “Il Ponte Druso prima e dopo la cura: non servono commenti.” Before: the stone balustrade and the columns with their eagles. After: a bare deck with an iron railing, a small car crossing, the tower of the former GIL behind.
The essay's author preferred the first: “le balaustre in pietra e le acquile del ponte Druso mi piacevano più delle attuali ringhiere in ferro”. The earlier photograph is undated and uncredited.
facts: Caption: 'Il Ponte Druso prima e dopo la cura: non servono commenti. Sullo sfondo il complesso ex GIL-femminile, minacciato negli scorsi anni di demolizione, rappresenta un bel esempio di architettura del razionalismo italiano.' [V] (notes 13, §12)
Bassetti: 'Così come le balaustre in pietra e le acquile del ponte Druso mi piacevano più delle attuali ringhiere in ferro.' [V] (notes 13, §12)

In the council on 6 Feb 1990 Holzmann (MSI-DN) called the bridge's stripping 'una distruzione inopinata che non ha avuto nessuna motivazione poi con l'allargamento della strada come si voleva contrabbandare a quel tempo' [V] (notes 13, §12)

Seen in the image: first picture, a stone bridge of arches over a stony river bed, a balustrade of pierced panels, columns rising from the piers with figures on top, a hill behind. Second picture, a road deck seen along its length with a plain railing on the right, a small car, street lamps and a tower block in the distance.
